newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuban official says sugar harvest can improve.
newsitem.headline: Cuban official says sugar harvest can improve.

text.p: Cuban vice-president Carlos Lage said Thursday that despite damage caused by Hurricane Lili, Cuba could still improve on last year's production in its forthcoming 1996-97 sugar cane harvest.
Hurricane Lili ripped through central and western areas of Cuba last Thursday and Friday, damaging crops, destroying more than 5,000 homes and cutting power lines and communications.

In an interview with the Communist Party newspaper Granma, Lage noted that affected crops included some 670,000 hectares (1.66 million acres) of sugar cane, just months ahead of the start of the 1996-97 sugar harvest.
But he reiterated comments earlier this week by the Sugar Ministry, saying that although cane was flattened or flooded, much of it will be useable for the harvest.
"These (affected sugar cane) plantations may have reduced yields but they are not lost," Lage said. He added they would largely recover with good weather and work to drain flooded fields.

Lage added that if sugar workers ensured minimal damage to the affected areas, and if the country also took into account the benefits of good rains to other areas of the country, it was still possible to continue improving Cuba's sugar production.

Before the hurricane, sugar experts had said Cuba could produce around 5.2 million to 5.3 million tonnes of sugar, up from 4.45 million tonnes in the 1995-96 harvest. Government officials had not given a target but had said the aim was to improve on 4.45 million tonnes.

Last year's harvest marked the halt of a steady decline in Cuba's key export earner since the early 1990s. Production in 1994-95 was a disastrous 3.3 million tonnes, the lowest harvest on the island for 50 years.
